title: Rubber stamp: electroformed nanoimprint stamper families replace EUV for capacitor holes
idea: Random stimulus 'rubber stamp' -> one e-beam-written master for the hexagonal storage-node hole array is copied, the way CD and DVD presses make stamper families, into father/mother/son nickel and quartz daughter templates. Jet-and-flash UV imprint then prints the periodic hole and landing-pad layers, and a 193i scanner handles only the aperiodic periphery.
why: Litho-bound scaling and capital (fact 4): the most periodic layers are the ones that carry most of the 5-7 EUV passes. Imprint tools cost ~$10-20M versus $200M+ for EUV, so the patterning cost of those layers could fall 3-5x; daughter templates spread the master's cost over millions of wafers.

title: Knitting: loop-end wordline layout deletes the SAQP cut mask
idea: Random stimulus 'knitting' (one yarn, closed loops, nothing cut) -> instead of cutting the closed ends of self-aligned quadruple-patterned spacer loops, which takes an extra critical mask, each loop is used as ONE electrical wordline that crosses two transistor rows. The active-area pattern is staggered so that each bitline contact sees only one gate in the loop, and the loop ends land on a sacrificial 'selvedge' strip that a blanket CMP trims away.
why: Removes 1-2 critical cut exposures, often EUV or double-patterned ArFi, per array layer, saving ~3-6% of wafer cost. Paired drive also halves the number of wordline drivers, which shrinks periphery (fact 7).

title: Honeycomb: anodic alumina pores self-register on landing pads as capacitor molds
idea: Random stimulus 'honeycomb' -> an aluminum film deposited over the landing-pad array is anodized at ~10-12 V, so pores nucleate at the pad-induced topographic dimples and grow straight down as a self-ordered hexagonal array with aspect ratio >100. The pores serve as the storage-capacitor mold, which needs no lithography and no high-AR plasma etch.
why: Attacks the capacitor charge wall (fact 1: AR 115 needed) and capital (fact 4). The mold litho and the most expensive etch step become a wet electrochemical bench costing <$1M, and AR rises from 70 to 120+ for ~1.7x more Cs.

title: Kaleidoscope: tabletop EUV Talbot self-imaging for periodic array layers
idea: Random stimulus 'kaleidoscope' (repeating images from simple optics) -> achromatic Talbot lithography: a compact 13.5 nm source shines through a simple transmission grating mask, and the self-imaging effect reproduces the periodic line/hole pattern at a set gap with no projection optics. It is used only for the fully periodic array layers; DUV handles cuts and periphery.
why: EUV single-supplier chokepoint and capital (fact 4): a mirror-less exposure tool could cost ~1/10 of a scanner and needs no reflective-mask infrastructure. It suits DRAM's array layers, which are almost perfectly periodic.

title: Croissant lamination: binary-tree bonding of tested half-stacks for 3D DRAM
idea: Random stimulus 'croissant' (fold dough, layers double) -> 3D DRAM tiers are built as single-crystal SOI-like silicon layers by smart-cut transfer, merged pairwise in parallel (1+1 -> 2, 2+2 -> 4, ... -> 32). Every sub-stack is e-beam- and probe-tested before merging, so bad half-stacks are discarded early instead of poisoning a finished 32-tier wafer.
why: No manufacturable 3D cell (fact 2): bonded layers give perfect lateral-transistor silicon without Si/SiGe superlattice epitaxy. Tree merging cuts serial cycle time from N to log2(N) bond steps and turns multiplicative tier-yield loss into screened yield.

title: Food truck: periphery-as-a-service from U.S. mature-node logic fabs
idea: Random stimulus 'food truck' (cook elsewhere, serve on site) -> the array wafer, which carries the EUV and capacitor steps, is made in a lean array-only fab. The CMOS periphery wafer (sense amps, decoders, I/O) is bought from existing U.S. 28-40 nm logic foundries and hybrid-bonded wafer-to-wafer.
why: Periphery is ~49% of the die (fact 7) yet needs no DRAM-specific tools. Moving it to depreciated U.S. logic capacity cuts DRAM-fab capex per bit ~30-40% and creates a U.S. supply path without a $15B fab.

title: Bamboo: grow vertical access transistors by in-situ-doped selective epitaxy
idea: Random stimulus 'bamboo' (grows in segments from a node) -> vertical channel transistors for 4F2 cells are grown, not etched: single-crystal silicon pillars are selectively epitaxied up through spacer-shrunk holes in an oxide template, switching dopant gas mid-growth to form n+/p/n+ junctions with abrupt profiles.
why: Removes the high-AR pillar etch and 2-3 implant/anneal steps. Grown sidewalls are damage-free, which narrows the leakage tail (fact 3), and the 4F2 layout gives 1.5x density over 6F2 without a node shrink.

title: Coral reef: electrolytic bottom-up superfill replaces CVD tungsten wordlines
idea: Random stimulus 'coral' (structures grown by electrochemical accretion from seawater) -> buried wordlines, bitline contacts and landing pads are filled by additive-driven bottom-up electroplating of Ru or Co on a sub-nm seed, the way copper damascene superfill works. This replaces WF6 CVD tungsten fill.
why: Scarce-resource intensity (tungsten ~80% China) and tool capital: wet plating cells cost a fraction of CVD-W clusters. Ru/Co lines also have lower resistance at <15 nm width, so wordline delay and voltage drop fall ~20-30%.

title: Shower head: atmospheric spatial ALD for high-k and electrodes
idea: Random stimulus 'shower head' -> wafers glide under a gas-bearing head with alternating precursor/purge/oxidant slots at atmospheric pressure, so every pass is one ALD cycle with no pump-down. It replaces vacuum batch and single-wafer ALD for the ZrO2/HfO2 capacitor dielectric and TiN electrodes.
why: Tool capital and throughput: spatial ALD reaches 10-50x the deposition rate with no vacuum hardware. The capacitor module's many ALD steps could need ~3x fewer tools and less floor space.

title: Fingerprint: random self-assembled cells with a per-die learned address map
idea: Random stimulus 'fingerprint' (unique random pattern, identified after the fact) -> only coarse wordline/bitline grids are patterned with relaxed DUV, and storage elements form randomly at crossings from block-copolymer or nanoparticle self-assembly with no registration. A built-in self-test fingerprints each die and writes a remap table, so the controller addresses only crossings that captured a working cell.
why: Removes overlay and critical-litho requirements for the storage node (fact 4). The design accepts ~60-80% site occupancy in exchange for eliminating several EUV/ArFi layers; this trades 20-40% raw area for large capex savings.

title: Velcro: capillary self-alignment for massively parallel die-to-wafer HBM bonding
idea: Random stimulus 'Velcro' (rough placement, self-locking) -> dies are dropped roughly onto hydrophilic bonding sites wetted with a water film, and surface tension pulls each die to sub-micron alignment before direct hybrid bonding. Thousands of dies are placed in parallel instead of one at a time by precision bonders.
why: HBM TSV tax and capital (fact 6): high-accuracy D2W bonders run ~$3-5M each at low throughput. Fluidic placement could raise stacking throughput ~10x and allows yield-sorted known-good dies.

title: Escalator: continuous flow-line DRAM array fab instead of job shop
idea: Random stimulus 'escalator' (constant flow, no waiting) -> an array-only fab is laid out as a process-ordered linear line, with tools sized to takt time and vacuum or overhead transfer straight between steps. Wafers flow like an escalator rather than queueing in a randomized job shop.
why: Capital and time: DRAM cycle time is 60-90 days, mostly queueing. A flow line could cut it to ~20-25 days, reducing WIP inventory, working capital and the time from capex to revenue for a new U.S. entrant.

title: Vending machine: tool vendors own tools, fab pays per wafer pass
idea: Random stimulus 'vending machine' (owner stocks it, you pay per item) -> lithography, etch and deposition OEMs own and maintain tools inside a new DRAM fab and bill per wafer pass, with uptime guarantees, backed by a federal loan guarantee pool.
why: Capital intensity (depreciation ~55% of wafer cost, fact 4) turns into variable cost. A U.S. entrant's upfront capex could fall ~50-60%, and OEMs gain recurring revenue.

title: Lending library: used-DUV-only DRAM fab wins density by stacking
idea: Random stimulus 'library' (reuse old books) -> a U.S. fab is built from refurbished ArF immersion scanners and depreciated etch/dep tools at F~18-20 nm using SAQP. The lost density is recovered with a 4F2 vertical-channel cell plus two hybrid-bonded array layers, so the fab needs zero EUV.
why: EUV chokepoint and capital: used 193i tools cost ~$20-40M versus $200-400M per EUV scanner. Equal bits per mm2 could come at roughly 40% lower fab capex and with no export-controlled tools.

title: Swiss roll: self-rolling strained MIM film forms horizontal 3D DRAM capacitors
idea: Random stimulus 'Swiss roll' -> in lateral 3D DRAM tiers, a planar electrode/high-k/electrode stack with a built-in strain gradient is deposited, its sacrificial underlayer is released, and the stack curls into a multi-turn coil filling the tier cavity. Capacitor area grows 5-10x with only planar deposition.
why: Removes the lateral deep-recess etch that blocks 3D DRAM capacitors (fact 2). It could reach the ~5 fF target in a short footprint, so more tiers fit per height.

title: Zipper: controlled spalling reuses one CZ donor for many device layers
idea: Random stimulus 'zipper' (one crack propagates cleanly) -> a stressed nickel layer is plated on the donor and a crack is propagated at a set depth to peel a few-micron device layer onto a carrier. The donor is re-polished and reused 10-20 times, and the peeled thin layers go straight into HBM stacks without grinding.
why: Scarce resources (Spruce Pine >80% of high-purity quartz crucibles): ~10x fewer Czochralski boules per bit. It also removes back-grind and thinning steps from HBM manufacturing (fact 6).

title: Sand dunes: phase-locked ion-beam ripples as maskless pitch multipliers
idea: Random stimulus 'sand dunes' -> off-normal low-energy ion bombardment self-organizes surface ripples at 15-30 nm wavelength. A coarse 193i grating locks their phase, as graphoepitaxy does, so each DUV period breaks up into 4-6 ordered ripples that serve as a line hardmask, from a blanket exposure.
why: Litho capital (fact 4): a blanket ion-beam step (~$5M tool) replaces SAQP's repeated deposition/etch spacer loops or EUV for line/space array layers.

title: Washing machine: metal-assisted wet etching drills AR>100 capacitor holes
idea: Random stimulus 'washing machine' (a wet bath does the work) -> a patterned noble-metal mesh on silicon catalyzes local oxidation and dissolution in HF/H2O2, so the mesh sinks straight down and leaves a hole array with AR >100. Room-temperature wet tanks replace the plasma high-AR etch.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1) and capital: high-AR dielectric etch tools are among the costliest in the fab. MacEtch reaches very high aspect ratios with no plasma, so Cs could grow ~1.5x and etch capex fall >5x.

title: Sourdough starter: bacterial S-layer protein crystals as nanohole templates
idea: Random stimulus 'sourdough starter' (living culture self-propagates) -> recrystallized bacterial surface-layer proteins form 2D lattices with 10-30 nm spacing and hexagonal or square symmetry on wafers. They are used, after mineralization, as hardmask templates for storage-node hole arrays, and their crystallization is guided by a coarse prepattern.
why: Litho capital (fact 4): the protein is grown in fermenters for cents per wafer and gives a sub-20 nm periodic template with no EUV.

title: Lighthouse: one free-electron-laser EUV source shared by many scanners
idea: Random stimulus 'lighthouse' (one beam serves many ships) -> a U.S.-built energy-recovery-linac free-electron laser produces ~10 kW of EUV and splits it among 10-20 scanner bodies, replacing per-scanner tin-plasma sources with their CO2 drive lasers.
why: EUV single-supplier and cost (fact 4): source power and uptime limit EUV throughput. A shared FEL could double wafers per hour and cut EUV cost per layer ~40%, and it creates U.S. ownership of the source.

title: Traffic light: three-wavelength resist prints three self-aligned levels per coat
idea: Random stimulus 'traffic light' (three colors, one pole) -> a resist with three photoacid systems is tuned to 365, 248 and 193 nm. One coat is exposed through three masks and developed once into three-level topography, which transfers into a self-aligned contact, bitline and landing pad sequence.
why: Process step count and capital (fact 4): coat/develop/etch loops fall up to 3x for stacked levels, and the levels are self-aligned by construction, so overlay errors between them disappear.

title: Zebra stripes: superlattice edge transfer defines 8 nm bitlines without lithography
idea: Random stimulus 'zebra' -> an ALD/epitaxial superlattice of alternating materials (for example Si/SiGe) is cleaved and polished edge-on, selectively etched, metallized and stamped onto the wafer as a line array (superlattice nanowire pattern transfer). Film thickness, controlled to the angstrom, sets pitch and CD instead of optics.
why: Litho-bound scaling (fact 4): it enables sub-10 nm half-pitch bitline and wordline arrays with no EUV and near-zero CD variation, and the master superlattice is reusable.

title: Pasta extruder: drawn nanochannel glass bonded as capacitor mold
idea: Random stimulus 'pasta extruder' -> a glass preform with ordered core rods is drawn, stacked and redrawn several times, as microchannel plates are made, down to ~30 nm channels. Wafer-thin slices are bonded onto the transistor wafer, and the cores are etched out to leave AR >100 capacitor molds.
why: Capacitor charge wall and capital (facts 1 and 4): ~10^11 channels/cm2 are made by fiber drawing with zero litho, and the mold step moves out of the fab into a glass plant.

title: Fridge magnet: define MTJ bits by ion irradiation, not etching
idea: Random stimulus 'fridge magnet' (stripes magnetized into a continuous sheet) -> the STT-MRAM stack stays continuous, and He+/N+ or oxygen ions implanted through a DUV-patterned mask destroy perpendicular anisotropy and tunnel magnetoresistance in the gaps, isolating bits magnetically without ion-beam etching the stack.
why: Non-volatile MRAM with endurance >1e12. It removes the MTJ etch (sidewall redeposition shorts, the yield killer) and IBE tools, and could cut MTJ pitch from ~90 nm to ~45 nm at DUV, about 4x density.

title: Parking garage: idle 3D NAND lines build vertical 1T-nC ferroelectric stacks
idea: Random stimulus 'multi-storey parking garage' -> one access transistor at ground level with n HZO ferroelectric capacitors stacked as floors along a vertical plate pillar. It is built with the staircase, channel-hole and replacement-gate tools of 3D NAND fabs that sit idle in NAND down-cycles.
why: Non-volatile, ~1e12-1e15 endurance, ~10-50 ns. It reuses depreciated NAND capex, so near-zero new tools are needed, and 8-16 bits per transistor footprint gives a step change in density per litho layer.

title: Smoke detector: radioisotope micro-battery keeps low-leakage cells alive for decades
idea: Random stimulus 'smoke detector' (a tiny Am-241 source runs for decades) -> a Ni-63 or tritium betavoltaic cell in the module package supplies microwatts forever, refreshing an ultra-low-leakage gain-cell array whose retention is ~1000 s. Data survives loss of external power for ~decades with no new memory material.
why: Non-volatility comes from the package, with zero new process modules or fab capex. At 1000 s retention, refresh for a 16 Gb die is ~0.7 uW, which is within betavoltaic output, and the array keeps DRAM-class speed and unlimited endurance.

title: Tree rings: magnetic racetrack on vertical hole walls, one litho layer
idea: Random stimulus 'tree rings' (records stored along depth) -> a perpendicular magnetic multilayer is deposited conformally on the sidewall of each NAND-like vertical hole, and bits are stored as domains along the depth, shifted by current pulses to a read/write MTJ at the top. One hole lithography defines 32-128 bits.
why: Non-volatile, with unlimited domain-wall-shift endurance. Bits per litho step rise ~50x, which collapses mask and EUV cost per bit; access is ~20-80 ns.

title: Rice terraces: bevel-polish exposes all tiers for one-mask contacts
idea: Random stimulus 'rice terraces' -> instead of a 3D NAND-style staircase (many trim-etch loops) for a multi-tier ferroelectric or MRAM stack, a tilted-pad CMP or ion-beam bevel cuts a shallow ramp through all tiers at once, and every plate line is contacted on the ramp in a single lithography step.
why: For non-volatile 3D FeRAM and FeFET stacks, it replaces 10-30 staircase litho/trim cycles with one bevel plus one mask, cutting ~5-10% of wafer cost and much of the cycle time.

title: Sugar cube: water-dissolved sacrificial layer transfers epitaxial perovskite ferroelectric
idea: Random stimulus 'sugar cube' (dissolves in water) -> single-crystal BaTiO3 or PZT-class ferroelectric is grown at high temperature on a reusable SrTiO3 donor over a water-soluble Sr3Al2O6 layer. Dissolving that layer releases the membrane, which is bonded onto finished CMOS at <300 C.
why: Non-volatile FeRAM with epitaxial-quality films (endurance >1e12, Pr several times HZO). It decouples the high-temperature growth from CMOS, and the donor is reused, so no perovskite-compatible fab is needed.

title: Abacus beads: bistable NEMS cells made in DLP-style MEMS fabs
idea: Random stimulus 'abacus' (beads flip between two stable sides) -> each bit is a nanoscale torsion paddle latched in one of two tilted states by electrostatic hold and stiction-free landing tips, the way TI's DLP micromirror is, read capacitively. It is built by sacrificial-release processing in existing U.S. 200 mm MEMS fabs.
why: Non-volatile and immune to radiation. DMD hinges show >1e12 flips, so endurance is effectively unlimited, and the cells use only Al/oxide/amorphous Si and mature U.S. tools, with no EUV or scarce elements. Risk: scaling the pitch to ~100 nm.

title: Compass needle: voltage-controlled anisotropy lets one transistor serve many MTJs
idea: Random stimulus 'compass needle' (flipped by a field, no current) -> MTJs written by voltage-controlled magnetic anisotropy, with precessional switching at near-zero current. The access transistor no longer needs to be wide, so 8-16 MTJs share one transistor in a 1T-nMTJ string at relaxed 28-40 nm litho.
why: Non-volatile, with high endurance because no large current flows through the barrier. Transistor area per bit falls ~8x, which reaches DRAM-like density on mature U.S. logic nodes without EUV.

title: Stained glass: ferroelectric memory panels from Gen-8.5 display fabs
idea: Random stimulus 'stained glass' (large panes, assembled) -> 1T1C ferroelectric memory with IGZO thin-film transistors and HZO capacitors is made on 2.2 x 2.5 m glass panels in display fabs, then the panels are diced into CXL memory tiles for a capacity tier.
why: Non-volatile, ~1e11+ endurance. Panel area costs ~50-100x less per cm2 than 300 mm silicon, so even at ~1 um cell pitch a panel holds ~600+ GB, and idle LCD capacity becomes memory supply. Weaker on density and latency.

title: Thermos flask: NEM relay access device with vacuum-isolated storage node
idea: Random stimulus 'thermos' (a vacuum gap stops heat leaking) -> the access transistor of a DRAM-like cell is replaced by a nano-electromechanical relay whose open contact is a vacuum gap, and the storage node sits in a sealed air-gap cavity. Off-state leakage is essentially zero, so charge persists for years.
why: Turns the leakage tail into retention of years (non-volatile) and eliminates refresh and its circuitry (fact 3). Relays are made by low-temperature sacrificial release in BEOL at relaxed pitch, but contact endurance is the risk.

title: Two-slot piggy bank: finance NV-memory fabs from memory plus storage budgets
idea: Random stimulus 'piggy bank with two slots' -> because the product is non-volatile, it is sold to hyperscalers as both the DRAM tier and a hot-storage/write-cache tier. Take-or-pay prepurchase agreements from both budgets are pooled into securitized fab financing.
why: Capital intensity: drawing on two procurement budgets doubles the addressable spend that backs one fab, lowers the cost of capital, and makes a $5-8B U.S. NV-memory fab financeable years sooner.

title: Rental car: standalone MRAM modules from existing U.S. eMRAM foundry lines
idea: Random stimulus 'rental car' (use someone else's fleet now) -> STT-MRAM modules (CXL/DIMM) are taped out on embedded-MRAM processes already qualified at U.S. 22 nm foundry lines, using spare BEOL capacity with no new fab.
why: Near-zero capex and immediate U.S. manufacturability. Density is ~10-20x below DRAM, so it serves as a bridge tier for persistent metadata, KV caches and checkpoints, freeing DRAM bits during the shortage.

title: Keyboard matrix: selector-free self-rectifying FTJ crosspoint stacks, two masks per layer
idea: Random stimulus 'keyboard matrix' (keys at row/column crossings) -> a ferroelectric tunnel junction (thin HZO with asymmetric electrodes) rectifies by itself, so 4F2 crosspoint decks need only two line masks each. Eight decks are stacked with DUV SAQP, and a DRAM-front cache plus wear-leveling supply effectively unlimited endurance.
why: Non-volatile, with no transistor in the array and only ~2 masks per deck. Bits per mask rise several-fold versus 1T1C, and the design needs zero EUV.

title: Pearl: one seeded ferroelectric grain per cell kills variability
idea: Random stimulus 'pearl' (one crystal grows around one seed) -> a self-aligned nucleation seed (a ZrO2 or TiN facet) is planted at the bottom of each ferroelectric capacitor, so the HZO crystallizes as a single orthorhombic grain per cell instead of random multigrain.
why: Non-volatile FeRAM is currently sized for grain-induced variation of Pr and Ec. Single-grain cells could shrink 2-3x at the same litho (relaxed DUV instead of EUV) and cut wake-up and fatigue spread.

title: Toaster: millisecond flash-lamp anneals stack 32 ferroelectric tiers monolithically
idea: Random stimulus 'pop-up toaster' (brief surface heat) -> each newly deposited HZO tier is crystallized by a 1-20 ms xenon flash or laser that heats only the top ~100 nm to >600 C while buried tiers and CMOS stay <400 C. This enables monolithic 32-tier FeRAM/FeFET stacking in BEOL.
why: Non-volatile 3D memory without wafer bonding. Density per litho area scales with tier count, and wafer cost per bit falls ~5-10x at 32 tiers.

title: Piezo lighter: sputtered AlScN ferroelectric made in U.S. RF-filter fabs
idea: Random stimulus 'piezo lighter' -> ferroelectric AlScN (Pr >100 uC/cm2) is deposited by plain reactive sputtering at <400 C, as in the BAW filter fabs of U.S. RF companies. It is used as the storage element of 1T1C non-volatile cells, and its giant Pr gives enough signal charge from a planar, non-pillar capacitor.
why: Non-volatile. It eliminates the high-AR capacitor mold and the ALD tools (facts 1 and 4) and reuses U.S. RF sputter capacity. Endurance (~1e7 today) needs a DRAM cache front and materials work.

title: Recipe card: open national NV-memory process kit for 200mm fabs
idea: Random stimulus 'recipe card' -> a federally funded lab line publishes a complete, licensable FeRAM/MRAM-on-CMOS process module (recipes, PDK, test and reliability data) designed for 200 mm and 300 mm mature tools. Any U.S. fab can then add a non-volatile memory product.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital: it lowers the barrier from billions in development to tens of millions in module tools and spreads NV capacity across ~20 existing U.S. fabs.

title: Snow globe: core-shell magnetic nanoparticles settle into wells as bits
idea: Random stimulus 'snow globe' (particles settle where they belong) -> chemically synthesized FePt-core/MgO-shell nanoparticles (each one a high-anisotropy bit with its own tunnel barrier) are fluidically self-assembled into DUV-defined wells over fixed-layer electrodes, then top-contacted and written with thermally assisted spin torque.
why: Non-volatile MRAM-class bits made by beaker chemistry instead of MTJ sputter and etch tools. It could cut the magnetic-module capex >10x, with 10-year retention at 5 nm from FePt anisotropy.

title: Bicycle gears: one ferroelectric capacitor shifts between DRAM mode and NV mode
idea: Random stimulus 'bicycle gears' -> a near-antiferroelectric HZO cell runs as a fast linear high-k (k~40) DRAM capacitor during operation, with unlimited endurance because the polarization does not switch. On a power-fail signal, a plate-line pulse shifts every row into remanent polarization, so the polarization flips only at power events.
why: Non-volatile when it matters and unlimited endurance in normal use. One capacitor module replaces separate DRAM plus NVDIMM/flash backup, and high k eases the charge wall (fact 1).

title: Mail sorting: NV array stores its own repair map, fuse-free
idea: Random stimulus 'mail sorting room' (routing table kept on site) -> because the cells are non-volatile, redundancy maps, trim codes and sense-amp offsets are written into reserved rows of the array itself. This eliminates the laser-fuse repair step, the e-fuse banks and their test-floor tools, and allows in-field re-repair.
why: Periphery (fact 7) shrinks ~2-4% of die area, laser repair tools leave the back-end, and test cost falls. Field self-repair raises effective yield.

title: Lava lamp: self-assembled multiferroic nanopillars define bits without lithography
idea: Random stimulus 'lava lamp' (blobs separate by themselves) -> co-deposition of BiFeO3 and CoFe2O4 spontaneously phase-separates into vertical magnetic nanopillars about 20 nm apart in a ferroelectric matrix. Each pillar is a non-volatile bit switched by electric-field strain, and a coarse template guides pillar positions.
why: Removes bit-defining lithography and MTJ etch, and gives voltage-written, attojoule-class switching. Risks: growth temperature and registration require the layer to be grown on a template and then bonded.

title: Ice hotel: platinum-group-free, tungsten-free MTJ stack from abundant elements
idea: Random stimulus 'ice hotel' (built only from local, abundant material) -> a heavy-metal-free STT stack: MnN exchange-bias pinning instead of IrMn or PtMn, a Cr spacer synthetic antiferromagnet instead of Ru, an Fe-rich FeB/MgO free layer, and Mo caps instead of Ta or W.
why: Scarce-resource intensity: removes Ir, Pt and Ru (PGM chokepoints) and tungsten (China ~80%) from non-volatile MRAM, using only sputter targets sourced in the U.S. and allies, with targets ~30% cheaper.

title: Orrery: orbital-current torque in light metals replaces heavy-metal SOT lines
idea: Random stimulus 'orrery' (orbits drive the motion) -> SOT-MRAM write lines use the orbital Hall effect in abundant light metals (Ti, Cr or oxidized Cu), with a Ni-based conversion layer that turns orbital current into torque on the free layer. This replaces beta-tungsten, Pt or Ta spin-Hall lines.
why: Non-volatile SOT-MRAM keeps unlimited endurance (no barrier current) and sub-ns writes. It removes tungsten and PGM dependence, and lower-resistivity lines cut write energy and driver area.
